scenes.heading: Volume of prisms and cylinders
scenes.say: How much water fits in a tank? How much chocolate is in a triangular bar? One simple rule works for every prism and every cylinder. Let's learn it.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: A loaf of sliced bread: every slice is the same shape
scenes.science: Prism: the same cross-section all the way through. V = A × h
scenes.breaks: A real loaf has a domed top and uneven end slices, but a true prism is exactly the same at every slice.
scenes.say: Think of a loaf of sliced bread. Every slice is the same shape. To find how much bread there is, take the area of one slice and multiply by the length of the loaf. Prisms and cylinders work exactly the same way.

scenes.heading: The volume rule
scenes.say: Volume equals A times h. A is the area of the cross-section, the end face. h is the distance between the two ends. For a cylinder, the end is a circle, so the volume is pi r squared h.
scenes.caption: V = A × h. A is the area of the end face; h is the distance between the ends. Cylinder: V = πr²h.

scenes.heading: Find the cross-section
notes: The shaded end is the cross-section A
h is the distance between the ends
scenes.say: Look at this prism. The shaded end face is the cross-section, A. Every slice through the prism is this same shape. The distance between the two ends is h.

scenes.heading: Triangular prism
scenes.question: Triangle cross-section with base 6 cm and height 4 cm. The prism is 10 cm long. Find its volume.
scenes.say: A triangular prism has a triangle end with base six and height four centimetres. Its area is twelve square centimetres. Multiply by the length, ten centimetres. The volume is one hundred and twenty cubic centimetres.
scenes.caption: Triangle end: ½ × 6 × 4 = 12 cm². Times the 10 cm length: V = 120 cm³.

scenes.heading: Cross-section × length
scenes.say: Here's the triangular prism. First the triangle end, with base six and dashed height four. Then the length, ten centimetres, going back.
scenes.caption: First the triangle end, base 6 cm and height 4 cm. Then the length, 10 cm, going back.

scenes.heading: Cylinder
scenes.question: Find the volume of a cylinder with radius 3 cm and height 10 cm, to 1 decimal place.
scenes.say: A cylinder has radius three and height ten centimetres. The circle's area is pi times three squared, nine pi. Times ten gives ninety pi, which is about two hundred and eighty-two point seven cubic centimetres.
scenes.caption: Circle end: π × 3² = 9π cm². Times 10: 90π ≈ 282.7 cm³.

scenes.heading: Tank in litres
scenes.question: A cylindrical tank has diameter 1.2 m and height 1.5 m. How many litres, to the nearest litre?
scenes.say: A water tank has diameter one point two metres and height one point five. Halve the diameter: radius nought point six. The volume is about one point six nine six five cubic metres. Each cubic metre is a thousand litres, so it holds about one thousand six hundred and ninety-six litres.
scenes.caption: r = 0.6 m. V = π × 0.6² × 1.5 ≈ 1.6965 m³. Times 1000: about 1696 L.

scenes.heading: Every time
steps: Check units: cm³, m³ or litres
scenes.say: Here's the method every time. Find the cross-section. Work out its area. Multiply by the length. Then check your units, and convert to litres if the question asks.

Quick recap. For any prism, volume is the cross-section area times the length. For a cylinder, it's pi r squared h, so halve the diameter first. And one cubic metre is a thousand litres. Now try the practice questions!
scenes.caption: Prism: V = A × h. Cylinder: V = πr²h, so halve the diameter first. 1 m³ = 1000 L. Now try the practice questions!
